opus-5.5.text:
I think at Stanford the relationship is much closer to a partnership than a hierarchy. When I was there, what struck me most was that advisers didn't really treat PhD students as people who simply execute their ideas. They treated you as a junior colleague, someone whose job is eventually to know more about your specific problem than they do.

Of course, it varies a lot from lab to lab. Some advisers are very hands-on: they meet you every week, they go through your code, they help you shape the paper line by line. Others are much more hands-off. They give you a direction, maybe introduce you to the right people, and then expect you to come back when you have something interesting. Neither style is better in itself. What matters is whether it fits the student.

What I learned is that the most important thing an adviser gives you is not a specific idea but taste: how to judge which problems are worth working on, what a good result looks like, when to push further and when to let something go. You absorb that through many conversations, often informal ones, sometimes arguments. At Stanford students were encouraged to disagree. If you thought your adviser was wrong, you were expected to say so and back it up. A good adviser actually enjoys that.

There's also a kind of trust involved. The adviser is betting on you for five or six years, and you're betting part of your life on them. So I'd say it's a mutual investment. The healthiest relationships I saw were the ones where, by the end, the student had become independent enough that the adviser was learning from them. That, I think, is the real goal of a PhD.

r001.rationale: The response describes the relationship as a mutual investment, with each side betting on the other, but does not characterize it as mutual selection.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to understand is that at Stanford, the adviser isn't really a boss, and the student isn't really an employee. It's closer to an apprenticeship, but an apprenticeship where the apprentice is expected to eventually disagree with the master.

When I was doing my PhD, my adviser almost never told me what to do. He would ask questions. He'd ask why I believed something, or what would happen if the assumption were wrong, and then he'd let me go struggle with it for two weeks. At the time it felt inefficient, even a little cruel. Later I understood that this was the entire point. The adviser's job is not to transfer knowledge, it's to transfer taste. Taste for which problems are worth working on, taste for when a result is actually surprising versus just technically correct. You can't teach that by giving instructions. You can only teach it by letting someone make decisions and then reacting honestly to those decisions.

The second thing is that the relationship is very much a two-way bet. The adviser is betting four or five years of their reputation and funding on you. You're betting the most formative years of your intellectual life on them. So the good advisers I saw were quite careful about who they took, and good students were equally careful about who they chose. People talk about the admissions process, but honestly the matching process after admission matters more. Students rotate, they talk to senior students in the lab, they figure out whether this professor actually shows up to meetings or disappears for a semester.

And the third thing, which I think is different from a lot of Chinese academic culture, is that there's an expectation that the student will eventually outgrow the adviser in some direction. The best outcome for a Stanford professor is not a student who faithfully extends their research agenda. It's a student who goes somewhere the professor couldn't have gone. The professors say this out loud. They're proud when a student contradicts them in a paper. That took me some time to get used to, because my instinct was to be deferential, and I slowly realized that deference was actually being read as a lack of ideas.

Of course, that's the ideal version. There are bad advisers at Stanford too, people who treat students as labor, and the power asymmetry is real. The student can't really leave without losing years. But the culture at least points in the right direction, and the culture is strong enough that it constrains the bad actors somewhat. Senior faculty notice when a lab has students who keep quitting. So I'd say the relationship is best understood as a long, slightly uncomfortable collaboration where the goal is to make the junior partner independent as fast as possible.

r001.rationale: The response says advisers are careful about whom they take and students are equally careful about whom they choose, describing the relationship as a mutual selection process.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a relationship that combines mentorship and collaboration. Your adviser helps you develop judgment: how to choose a worthwhile problem, how to approach it, and how to tell whether you’re making progress. But as a PhD student, you also need to take ownership of the research. You can question your adviser’s assumptions and bring your own ideas to the discussion.

I wouldn’t say there’s one model that describes every adviser at Stanford. Some are more hands-on, while others give students a lot of independence. What matters is whether you can communicate openly and whether the relationship helps you become an independent researcher.

r001.rationale: It describes mentorship, collaboration, student ownership, and variation among advisers, but does not characterize the relationship as involving mutual selection.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a relationship that evolves. Early in the PhD, your adviser helps you identify important questions and develop the skills to pursue them. As you grow, you take more ownership of the research, and the relationship becomes more like a collaboration between colleagues.

At Stanford, I’d be careful about describing one model, because advisers have different styles. But the healthiest relationship combines independence with support: the student can challenge ideas, ask for help, and discuss what isn’t working. The adviser provides guidance without making every decision. Ultimately, the goal is for the student to become an independent researcher.

r001.rationale: The response describes an evolving, supportive relationship that becomes collaborative, but does not characterize it as one of mutual selection.
